    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-02 | When would SQL doubles, CDS doubles and RAP BO doubles give misleading confidence?
column2:
Short answer
Test doubles replace particular dependencies; they do not prove the whole application works. SQL doubles help isolate database access, CDS doubles help test CDS logic, and RAP BO doubles can replace another object's EML behavior. I choose the double for the rule being tested. Real persistence, permissions and service behavior still need suitable integration checks.

Reasoning and example
A pricing calculation reads a table. A SQL double can supply controlled prices so the test checks the calculation without depending on production data. That test does not prove an external action is still compatible. Likewise, a fake EML error response can test how a consumer handles failure, but it does not test the provider that would produce the real error.

I state what each test actually executes and replaces. A generic BO buffer double does not run arbitrary custom provider logic, and access-control behavior needs explicit checks. Focused integration tests then cover the real save, authorization and service path. A more advanced-looking double does not automatically supply stronger evidence.

Avoid this mistake
A more sophisticated double does not automatically provide broader integration evidence.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which behavior is replaced by the double?
  • Which important behavior still needs a real integration test?
Strong answer criteria
  • Chooses doubles for the dependency being replaced
  • Explains what the test does not execute
  • Checks the real integration separately
Verification evidence
Record what each test covers, then verify one relevant path through the real provider and service.

column1: OPS-03 | A bulk EML action processes ten requests and rejects two. What should its test assert?
column2:
Short answer
I check which specific requests succeeded or failed, using their identities rather than row positions. I verify FAILED entries, message targets and the resulting data. I also test whether the chosen operation should allow partial success or require everything to succeed together. A successful interaction is not enough if saving later rejects the change.

Reasoning and example
I send ten requests with deliberately nonsequential keys. Two have different invalid values. The test checks that exactly those identities appear as failed, that each message points to the right request and that valid requests receive the intended treatment. Reordering inputs helps reveal code that accidentally matches results by row number.

Next, I test a failure during save after the interaction step appeared successful. The consumer must not report that object as permanently completed. I inspect buffered and saved state according to the supported test boundary. The expected all-or-nothing or partial-result rule must be defined first; counting ten messages cannot tell me whether ten operations were handled correctly.

Avoid this mistake
Ten messages do not prove ten correct results. Match outcomes to the actual request identities.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Must all requests succeed together, or is partial success allowed here?
  • How will the test detect a failure that happens only during save?
Strong answer criteria
  • Matches every result to its input identity
  • Checks interaction results and saved data separately
  • Tests the intended all-or-nothing or partial-success rule
Verification evidence
Show which requests should succeed or fail, where their messages point and which rows remain after each failure case.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-04 | A draft test passes when run alone but fails after another test. What would you inspect?
column2:
Short answer
I look for state left behind by the earlier test. That can include draft or active data, transaction buffers, locks and configured test-double responses. Each test should set up its own state and clean up through supported test mechanisms. I do not add random commits to hide the problem, because that can change what the test proves.

Reasoning and example
Two tests use request 4711. The first leaves a draft or a configured double response behind, while the second assumes a clean active request. Running the second alone works; running the pair fails. I run them in the opposite order and inspect setup and teardown to find the shared state.

Distinct fixture keys can help confirm the cause, but the final fix should still manage the test environment correctly. I check active and draft identities separately, release supported resources and reset doubles as required. A fixture for an active instance is not automatically a valid draft fixture. An order-dependent pass is weak evidence of correct draft behavior.

Avoid this mistake
A test that depends on execution order is unreliable evidence for draft behavior.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Are active and draft transactional keys distinct?
  • Which setup/teardown resource is shared?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes active and draft identities
  • Resets the test resources correctly
  • Proves tests do not depend on their order
Verification evidence
Run the tests separately, in both orders and in the suite. Keep results showing they behave consistently.

Read and verify

    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-05 | How do you prove optimistic concurrency rather than merely calling the same update twice?
column2:
Short answer
I use two independent clients that read the same version before either saves. The first update should succeed; the second should be rejected when it sends the old ETag. I check that the first user's data remains intact. Draft locks and the draft total ETag need separate tests because they protect different parts of the editing flow.

Reasoning and example
Alice and Ben both read one entity instance and keep its ETag. Alice changes it and saves. Ben then updates that same instance with his old token. The expected result is a stale-version rejection, not an overwrite. If Ben rereads first, he gets the new token and the test no longer exercises a stale writer.

For draft, I separately test editing while an exclusive lock is valid and resuming after it expires. A child-only change to active data should be considered by the configured draft total ETag check. That is different from the entity-level If-Match test. Two updates inside one shared transaction do not reproduce two users with independent versions.

Avoid this mistake
Two updates in one shared transaction are not a realistic two-user concurrency test.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which token protects this entity update?
  • What separate case should the draft total ETag test cover?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses independent clients or sessions
  • Sends an intentionally old version token
  • Checks that rejected updates leave data intact
Verification evidence
Record each client version, request, response and final value from the controlled two-user test.

Read and verify
  • SAP total ETag and draft concurrency
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-06 | Fiori still displays an old total after a successful action. How do you separate UI refresh from backend correctness?
column2:
Short answer
I first read the business object again to see whether the server saved the right value. If the value is wrong there, I investigate the backend calculation. If it is right, I check what the UI refreshes after the action. The action result, side effects and deployed metadata must tell the client what changed.

Reasoning and example
An item quantity changes and the server recalculates the order total, but the original Fiori screen still shows the old amount. I compare a direct read, a new UI session and the original session's network requests. If both fresh reads show the correct total, the likely problem is that the original screen did not request the changed field.

I inspect the supported side-effect declaration and action result, then test a targeted refresh with the actual deployed metadata. I do not add a second total calculation in the browser to hide a backend problem. Another commit or a full-page reload may mask the symptom without fixing the missing refresh behavior.

Avoid this mistake
A page reload workaround does not explain whether the backend or refresh contract was defective.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What does a fresh service read return?
  • Which request should refresh the affected property?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks the value actually held by the backend
  • Inspects metadata and network requests
  • Keeps the business calculation on the server
Verification evidence
Record the action and later reads, showing values before and after in the actual app.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP side effects
    Check which field or action triggers a refresh, what gets refreshed and whether the actual UI supports it.

column1: OPS-07 | A RAP list becomes slow after enabling count and expanding children. What do you measure first?
column2:
Short answer
I measure where the request spends its time: selecting rows, counting, loading children or doing extra ABAP and remote work. I use representative data and the affected user's permissions. Then I change the largest proven cost and repeat the same test. I preserve filtering, count correctness and access checks while reducing unnecessary work.

Reasoning and example
A page shows only 20 orders, but its count scans millions of allowed records and its expansion loads many child items. I compare a page-only request, a request with count and one with expansion. Traces show database time, application time, rows and any remote calls, so I can see which addition causes the delay.

I repeat the measurement with a restricted user because authorization filtering can change the database work. If expansion is the issue, the consumer may not need every child on the first screen. If count dominates, changing a small handler calculation will do little. I compare before and after using the same parameters and volume.

Avoid this mistake
Do not optimize the shortest visible SELECT before finding the dominant request cost.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Is count more expensive than the page?
  • What changes for an authorization-restricted user?
Strong answer criteria
  • Measures the separate parts of the request
  • Uses realistic data and user permissions
  • Keeps correct results and access checks while improving speed
Verification evidence
Keep comparable before-and-after traces showing total time, rows and calls.

Read and verify

column1: OPS-08 | A custom entity calls a remote API once for every returned row. How would you remove the N+1 pattern?
column2:
Short answer
I look for a supported bulk request instead of one remote call per row. I fetch only the references needed for the current result and limit request size. A cache is an option only with clear freshness and access rules. I still handle missing results, throttling and partial failures rather than hide them behind a faster response.

Reasoning and example
A page reads 50 orders and then calls a remote service once for each supplier. Together with the original read, that is 51 calls. A supported bulk endpoint may fetch the needed supplier references in one request. I remove duplicate keys and keep the batch within the service's limits instead of downloading every supplier.

The bulk response may still contain missing references or individual errors. I test those cases and rate limits, not just the reduced call count. If caching is needed, I define how long values remain valid and which user or tenant may reuse them. A shared cache must not expose one customer's data to another.

Avoid this mistake
An unbounded cache can trade latency for stale or cross-user data leakage.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is the maximum request size?
  • How are partial remote failures represented?
Strong answer criteria
  • Uses bulk requests with size limits
  • Defines cache freshness and who may reuse data
  • Handles missing results and rate limits
Verification evidence
Measure remote calls and transferred rows, including tests for missing data and rate limits.

Read and verify
  • SAP: Implementing an Unmanaged Query
    Check the supported request options and target release. Test bulk reads and caching for correct results, access control and speed in your own scenario.

column1: OPS-09 | A service works in development but fails after transport. What evidence should the handoff have included?
column2:
Short answer
A transport moves code, but the service may also need configuration, roles, communication setup and frontend deployment. I verify the active version and dependencies in the target system. The handoff should name these requirements and their owners. A working development preview or successful import does not prove that the real production user can use the service.

Reasoning and example
The RAP behavior activates after import, but an action fails because the destination or communication arrangement is missing. In another system, the endpoint exists but the intended user's role does not grant access. These are different failures from a defect in the business calculation, so I inspect the actual target setup before changing code.

The handoff should list the code and non-code prerequisites, installation order and a small end-to-end check. I verify the imported revision, service exposure, communication settings and consuming identity. Each item needs a responsible person and an observed result. Publishing a binding locally in development does not establish a usable production endpoint.

Avoid this mistake
A successful transport import does not prove that the service works for its real users.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which required items are configuration rather than source?
  • Who verifies the real consuming identity?
Strong answer criteria
  • Lists code and required configuration separately
  • Checks the version and setup in the target
  • Names who owns each operating requirement
Verification evidence
Record actual endpoint, role, communication and service-test results in the target readiness checklist.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP service binding
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-10 | How would you evolve a released RAP service when an action needs a new mandatory input?
column2:
Short answer
A new required parameter can break every existing caller that does not send it. I check whether a valid optional value or default can preserve old behavior. If not, I plan a new operation or version and a controlled migration. The change must meet the real business rule while giving consumers an explicit path to update.

Reasoning and example
An approval action now needs a legal justification. Old clients have no field for it. Supplying an empty default would keep calls running but might violate the new requirement, so technical compatibility alone is not enough. I agree a supported transition that respects when the new business rule must take effect.

That may involve a successor action, an announced retirement date and updates to both UI and integration clients. I test generated clients, metadata-driven screens and direct API consumers separately. I track actual use of the old operation before retiring it where the policy permits a transition. Successful server activation does not prove that existing requests still work.

Avoid this mistake
A changed action can activate successfully while still breaking existing callers.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Is a default legally/business valid?
  • How do you know which consumers still use the old contract?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explains why old callers may break
  • Plans a clear migration
  • Tests existing consumers
Verification evidence
Run old and new client tests, and track use of the old operation before retiring it.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP service binding
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-11 | A remote approval succeeded, but the RAP caller timed out. How should an operator recover?
column2:
Short answer
A timeout leaves the result unknown until I check it. I use the request's stable reference to find the remote approval before submitting again. If it exists, recovery should reuse that result. If it cannot be determined, the case needs a visible status and an owner. Local rollback cannot erase an approval already committed remotely.

Reasoning and example
The remote workflow creates approval 9001, but its response never reaches the RAP caller. A new creation request could start approval 9002 for the same submission. I query by the original reference or use the service's documented idempotency rule so a retry returns or reuses the first result. The local app records the resolved workflow link.

If the remote outcome cannot be queried, I keep a durable recovery record and use the agreed operator or compensation procedure. I also test a late duplicate callback and a callback for a request version that has since changed. A delayed response must not approve stale local data or repeat an already completed decision.

Avoid this mistake
A timeout is not evidence that the other system performed no work.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which stable reference identifies the original request?
  • Who investigates when the remote outcome cannot be queried?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes unknown from failed
  • Finds the original result before unsafe retry
  • Handles duplicate and outdated callbacks
Verification evidence
Simulate a lost response. Verify one intended business effect and a visible status from which recovery is possible.

Read and verify

    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-12 | A failed save leaves no business record, but support still needs diagnostics. How would you log it safely?
column2:
Short answer
I separate business audit records from technical diagnostics and user messages. A log written inside a rolled-back transaction may disappear too. I use supported monitoring for diagnostics that must survive, rather than add a commit inside RAP behavior code. Logs should identify the failed request without exposing secrets or claiming that a rejected business change succeeded.

Reasoning and example
An order fails validation. FAILED identifies the rejection and REPORTED supplies the relevant message, but no order is saved. Support still needs to connect that user error to the failed request. I use the available service or application monitoring facilities with their documented save and privacy behavior for that diagnostic purpose.

A business audit entry saying 'order submitted' has a different meaning and should accompany a successful business transition, not survive a rejected submission as a false fact. I test success and rollback and inspect which records remain. Adding COMMIT WORK in a handler just to keep a log would break RAP's ownership of transaction completion.

Avoid this mistake
Do not add COMMIT WORK inside a handler just to preserve a log entry.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Should this record remain after rollback?
  • Does it describe a technical failure or a completed business event?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates business audit from technical diagnostics
  • Lets RAP control transaction completion
  • Keeps sensitive values out of logs
Verification evidence
Test success and rollback, then inspect which supported messages and logs remain.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP business-object contract
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-13 | A production incident starts after a release. How do you contain it without making the data worse?
column2:
Short answer
I first limit the harmful processing through authorized operational controls and preserve the evidence. Then I identify the affected records and what has already committed. I choose a code fix, rollback or replay only after understanding those effects. Reverting code does not reverse business data, and replaying a backlog can repeat the damage.

Reasoning and example
A new Submit implementation starts duplicate remote approvals. I stop the affected scheduled initiation through the authorized control and record the release, request references and time window. Then I compare local requests with the remote approvals to find what was already created. Simply deploying the old code would not remove those duplicates.

After fixing duplicate handling, I test recovery on a controlled sample and reconcile existing approvals using supported business procedures. Only then do I resume the backlog, watching error counts and the rate of processing. The recovery plan needs a clear condition for resuming and an owner for unresolved records. Replaying everything before the fix could create even more approvals.

Avoid this mistake
Do not rerun the whole backlog while the duplicate-creation defect remains active.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which business changes have already been saved?
  • What result proves processing can safely resume?
Strong answer criteria
  • Stops harmful work before replaying it
  • Repairs code and business data separately
  • Defines when processing can safely resume
Verification evidence
Keep an incident timeline, a list of checked affected records and the result of a controlled replay after the fix.

Read and verify

column1: OPS-14 | What belongs in a RAP release gate beyond a passing ATC run?
column2:
Short answer
ATC is one check, not proof that the feature works. I also test the business rules, failures, permissions and integrations affected by the change. Changes involving saves or concurrency need matching rollback and conflict tests. I record the version and environment for each result, and clearly mark anything not run rather than count it as passed.

Reasoning and example
A release changes an action parameter and publishes a new approval event. I test existing callers against the new action, verify the event after a successful save and check duplicate delivery. I also test a user who must not submit. These checks address the risks of this change; they are more useful than repeating an unrelated checklist.

For a label-only adjustment, the required evidence would be much smaller. For this release, I also verify relevant performance, dependency compatibility and target configuration. ATC can find issues covered by its configured checks, but it cannot prove every business rule or external connection. The release record should show executed results, pending checks and their owners.

Avoid this mistake
Choose tests for the failure risks this change creates; a generic checklist alone is not enough.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which new failure mode did this change introduce?
  • Which result is pending rather than passed?
Strong answer criteria
  • Chooses checks for the risks of this change
  • Separates source checks from runtime tests
  • Records tested versions and pending checks
Verification evidence
Link each changed behavior to actual test results, responsible people and remaining risks.

column1: OPS-15 | A team advertises 95% coverage while never asserting FAILED or persisted state. How would you improve it?
column2:
Short answer
Coverage tells me which statements ran, not whether the results were correct. I add checks that fail when an important business rule is broken. For RAP, that can include rejected identities, messages, saved state and unwanted side effects. I then use coverage to find remaining gaps instead of adding meaningless code or repeating happy-path calls.

Reasoning and example
A test executes a validation for a missing account assignment and reports high coverage. However, it never checks FAILED, the message target or whether the invalid request can be saved. If I temporarily remove the rejection and the test still passes, it does not prove the validation works. I strengthen those assertions and restore the implementation.

I apply the same idea to successful processing: the test must check the expected state and absence of unintended changes. Coverage remains useful for locating paths we never executed, but the percentage is not the acceptance criterion by itself. A smaller set of failure-sensitive tests can provide stronger evidence than many calls without meaningful checks.

Avoid this mistake
High statement coverage can still miss a broken business rule.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Would the test fail if the business check were removed?
  • Which business rule matters more than increasing the coverage percentage?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks meaningful outcomes
  • Uses tests that fail when the rule is broken
  • Does not treat coverage as proof of correctness
Verification evidence
Demonstrate a test failing when rejection or saving is deliberately broken, then restore the code.

column1: OPS-16 | How would you prepare an extension for a platform upgrade?
column2:
Short answer
I list the APIs and extension points the application actually uses, then check what changes in the target release. I prioritize important business flows and known exceptions. Tests run against a representative target system and include affected consumers, permissions and behavior. Released APIs reduce some upgrade risk, but they do not remove the need to test our application.

Reasoning and example
An extension calls a classic dependency through a wrapper and also exposes a released service to another system. I give each dependency an owner and check its target-release status, including any deprecation or successor. A wrapper does not make an underlying upgrade risk disappear. Existing external clients need testing against the upgraded service too.

I then run focused regression tests for the affected metadata, draft behavior, authorization, performance and configuration. If an API must be replaced, the plan includes moving consumers before retiring the old path. Last year's ATC result is not evidence for this year's target release. I retain the tested versions and actual results for the important flows.

Avoid this mistake
Do not treat last year's clean ATC report as evidence for the new target release.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which dependencies create the biggest upgrade risk?
  • Does the application assume behavior the API documentation does not promise?
Strong answer criteria
  • Lists actual API and extension dependencies
  • Tests risks for the target release
  • Assigns owners for exceptions and deprecated APIs
Verification evidence
Record target versions, dependency classifications and regression results for the most important flows.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP feature and release overview
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: OPS-17 | A cloud job processes 500,000 records and times out. How would you redesign it?
column2:
Short answer
I split the work into limited-size packages that can restart safely. Each package has stable record IDs, a clear commit boundary and recorded progress. I use background or application-job features supported by the target system and limit parallel work. Recovery checks what actually completed, including changes that may have saved just before the job failed.

Reasoning and example
A pricing job finishes 20 packages and crashes during the next. On restart, it should not blindly repeat the completed work. I use recorded progress plus stable business references to distinguish completed, failed, pending and uncertain results. I also check whether a user edited a record after the original calculation so recovery does not overwrite newer data.

A critical test crashes between the business update and checkpoint handling. The design must detect the existing effect or repeat it safely; a checkpoint alone may not prove exactly-once execution. I tune package size and concurrency against database locks and remote limits. Moving one huge loop into a background job does not solve its restart problem.

Avoid this mistake
Moving a huge synchronous loop into a background job does not solve its transaction or restart design.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What is one package that can recover independently?
  • How does recovery avoid overwriting newer user changes?
Strong answer criteria
  • Limits package size and competing work
  • Defines how to find completed work after a crash
  • Uses supported cloud job features
Verification evidence
Simulate a failure inside a package, then verify restart, resource limits and final business totals.

Read and verify
  • SAP application job catalog and template
    Check how supported jobs run, then split the work into limited-size packages with clear restart points.

column1: OPS-18 | How would you communicate senior readiness when you can review code locally but cannot run SAP checks?
column2:
Short answer
I say clearly what I reviewed, what I prepared and what I actually ran. Local review can find defects and produce useful tests, but it cannot prove SAP activation or real runtime behavior. I provide exact target-system steps and expected results. Missing evidence stays pending; I do not replace it with a guessed pass or unrelated performance number.

Reasoning and example
For a RAP approval change, I can review the source and prepare tests for a valid submission, a denied user and a rejected save. I can also provide a two-session concurrency scenario and a service smoke test. The handoff states which source revision to transfer, which roles are needed and what each result should show.

The person with target access then runs syntax and activation checks, ATC and the relevant tests, returning logs tied to that revision and environment. Until then, prepared test code is not an executed result. A UI running against mocks also does not prove integration with RAP. Clear limits make the evidence more useful, not less credible.

Avoid this mistake
Do not present prepared test code or a mocked UI as successful SAP integration.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which claim can you prove now?
  • What exact target result would close the remaining risk?
Strong answer criteria
  • Clearly separates prepared and executed work
  • Provides runnable steps and expected results
  • Links results to the source revision and environment
Verification evidence
List prepared, executed and pending checks, with expected outcomes and the person responsible for each.

Read and verify
  • SAP RAP test frameworks and boundaries
    Use the documented framework rules to design these checks. These examples are proposed tests, not claimed SAP runtime results.

column1: GOV-01 | A project claims Level A because its frontend uses RAP. How would you assess the extension?
column2:
Short answer
Check the whole extension, including wrappers and the SAP objects they call. RAP and Fiori do not decide the Clean Core level. A depends on released contracts; B uses classified classic options; C uses internals; D uses non-recommended dependencies or techniques. Record the actual classification for each path on the target system. Do not call a mixed solution entirely Level A.

Reasoning and example
A RAP handler calls a custom wrapper, which then calls an internal SAP class. Looking only at the handler's released custom interface misses the underlying dependency. Assess the consumer and wrapper separately where appropriate, but include both in the delivered solution's dependency record. A customer namespace does not erase the risk.

Link each finding to the business capability it affects and the person responsible for maintaining it. Confirm the applicable API state, classification, and ATC result for the same source version. A passing UI test shows that a tested interaction worked, not that every call underneath uses Level A interfaces. State clearly what is included in any classification claim.

Avoid this mistake
RAP, BTP deployment, a customer namespace, or a green UI test is not proof that every underlying dependency is Level A.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What exactly is included in the claimed Level A scope?
  • How would you find dependencies hidden behind customer adapters?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines scope before classification
  • Traces indirect dependencies
  • Separates framework choice from API evidence
Verification evidence
An object-level dependency inventory with target-system release/classification evidence and the applicable ATC result for the same revision.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-02 | An API is released with C1. A team assumes that means Clean Core Level C and permission to expose it remotely. How do you respond?
column2:
Short answer
These are two different naming systems. C0 means Extend, C1 means Use System-Internally, and C2 means Use as Remote API. They are release-contract purposes, not Clean Core levels A to D. Check the object's visibility for the intended caller too. A C1 release does not by itself authorize remote exposure or classify the dependency as Level C.

Reasoning and example
A locally released class may be suitable for an on-stack application without being a remote API. If you build a custom remote service over it, you become the provider of a new interface. You must define authentication, business permissions, errors, transaction behavior, and how callers can rely on future versions.

The local API has not magically changed to C2, and your service does not inherit guarantees that its provider never made. Inspect API-state properties and documentation for the exact supported use. Keep the separate questions clear: what release purpose is allowed, who may consume it, and what Clean Core classification applies to the implementation's actual dependencies?

Avoid this mistake
C0/C1/C2 and Clean Core A/B/C/D are different classifications; release for one purpose does not release every possible usage.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which visibility must the API expose for this caller?
  • What responsibilities arise if you build a custom remote service over a local API?
Strong answer criteria
  • Names contracts accurately
  • Checks purpose and visibility
  • Recognizes new provider responsibilities
Verification evidence
ADT API-state properties, provider documentation, and a consumer design showing local use or an explicitly owned remote contract.

Read and verify
  • SAP release contracts, visibility, and API lifecycle states
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-03 | A team wraps an internal SAP function module and releases the wrapper. Has the technical debt disappeared?
column2:
Short answer
No. A wrapper can protect callers from some changes, but the underlying SAP dependency still has its original release status and upgrade risk. Record both the wrapper's public promise and its implementation dependency. Where allowed, give it an owner, regression tests, and a replacement plan. A useful wrapper hides unstable details; merely renaming the same internal interface adds little protection.

Reasoning and example
If the wrapper exposes the internal function module's structures unchanged, a provider change can still spread to every caller. A smaller request and result designed around the business need can contain more of that change inside the wrapper. Test those promised inputs, outcomes, and failures rather than only checking that the call returns.

A wrapper over a classified classic API can fall within the applicable Level B guidance. Wrapping an internal object does not make it a designated classic API. Keep the target-release assessment visible and define when a released replacement should be adopted. Your own release flag is a promise you maintain, not a way to change SAP's classification of its underlying object.

Avoid this mistake
A customer release flag does not turn an unreleased SAP dependency into a released SAP API or erase its classification.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which unstable details must stay behind the wrapper?
  • Who replaces the dependency when a released alternative becomes available?
Strong answer criteria
  • Records the underlying dependency risk
  • Provides a small stable interface
  • Names who replaces the dependency
Verification evidence
A wrapper dependency record, contract tests, an owner, and a documented replacement trigger with the current target-release assessment.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-04 | An urgent release needs an ATC exemption for an internal dependency. What makes the exception governable?
column2:
Short answer
Make the exception specific: business need, exact finding, source scope, target edition, alternatives, risk owner, and supporting tests. Give it an expiry or review trigger and a realistic fix plan. An ATC exemption changes how a finding is handled. It does not make forbidden code legal or turn the dependency into Level A. The release decision must accept the remaining risk explicitly.

Reasoning and example
An approved exception covers one read-only adapter. A later change adds a write through another internal call. That new risk must not silently inherit the old approval. Tie the exception to the relevant objects and finding category, rerun checks after changes, and revisit it when the provider or target release changes.

Keep security and transaction defects visible as separate decisions; they are not automatically accepted by a Clean Core waiver. State which tests reduce the risk and who will replace the dependency. An indefinite blanket exemption makes future changes hard to assess. A bounded exception lets the team deliver a justified need while preserving a clear limit on what was actually accepted.

Avoid this mistake
An approved exemption is not a reclassification to Level A and must not become a general permission to bypass ABAP Cloud restrictions.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What event invalidates this exception?
  • How do you prevent the approved scope from growing unnoticed?
Strong answer criteria
  • Limits what the exception covers and how long it lasts
  • Names who accepts and owns the risk
  • Distinguishes exempting a finding from permission to use an API
Verification evidence
An exception record linked to the exact ATC finding, source revision, release target, regression evidence, owner, and expiry or review trigger.

Read and verify
  • SAP ATC configuration and transport-release governance
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-05 | A Level B solution works in Private Edition. Can the same approval justify deploying it in Public Edition?
column2:
Short answer
No. A Level B decision does not override Public Edition's supported APIs, language rules, or extension options. Reassess the business need for that target using configuration, key-user tools, developer extensibility, and supported remote integration. Identify what cannot move and compare a supported redesign with keeping the current deployment. Even Level A does not guarantee identical capabilities across editions.

Reasoning and example
A Private Edition app uses a classic enhancement or SAP GUI-dependent component. It may have a justified role there but no supported equivalent in the proposed Public Edition scope. Moving its screen to BTP does not make an unavailable backend operation suddenly callable. Test the required business operation against actual target APIs.

Separate the parts that can be reused from those needing redesign. Record each missing capability and its effect on the process, then let the business compare alternatives with evidence. Prior approval of a dependency in one landscape is not permission in another. Classification helps assess risk; product availability and technical restrictions still determine which solution can be built.

Avoid this mistake
Level B is not a universal deployment permission, and Level A design does not guarantee identical API coverage across editions.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which part of the solution is genuinely portable?
  • What evidence would justify keeping a private-edition dependency?
Strong answer criteria
  • Checks target-edition constraints
  • Separates classification from portability
  • Offers supported redesign options
Verification evidence
An edition capability comparison with verified target APIs, extension points, and a documented functional gap for each nonportable component.

Read and verify
  • SAP extensibility options by environment and language version
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-06 | You have thousands of custom objects and a limited upgrade budget. How would you prioritize remediation?
column2:
Short answer
Prioritize by actual use, business importance, dependency risk, target-upgrade changes, and effort. Validate unused-code candidates before retiring them. Investigate high-impact non-recommended or changed internal paths early, and give remaining work owners and acceptance criteria. Do not rank only by object count or execution frequency. One critical posting dependency may matter more than hundreds of small utilities.

Reasoning and example
A year-end report has no executions in a three-month trace. Deleting it based on that trace alone can cause an outage at closing time. An emergency posting tool may run only once a year and still be essential when it is needed. Combine usage evidence with process-owner confirmation and the limits of the observation period.

Then compare target-upgrade changes with business impact and replacement cost. A daily financial dependency that changes in the target release may deserve urgent attention, while an unaffected lower-risk utility can wait. Record why each item has its priority and how success will be tested. A large findings count is not yet a useful remediation plan.

Avoid this mistake
Do not equate low execution frequency with low business importance or treat every finding as equal remediation work.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you avoid retiring seasonal functionality?
  • What makes one Level C dependency more urgent than another?
Strong answer criteria
  • Combines usage with business importance
  • Uses evidence about changes in the target release
  • Prioritizes work with clear owners
Verification evidence
A ranked remediation portfolio with usage-window limitations, business-owner decisions, dependency impact, estimated effort, and target-release tests.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-07 | No released API supports a required business operation. What would your escalation contain?
column2:
Short answer
Describe the business operation you need, the target product and release, and why existing supported options do not meet it. Include transaction behavior, permissions, expected volume, and failure needs. Provide a small reproducible example where helpful. Ask for a supported capability rather than simply a table release. Meanwhile, choose an explicit interim process, scope change, or permitted governed alternative.

Reasoning and example
Instead of saying release this table, explain that the application must close a document with the right validations, permissions, and failure response. Show which APIs and extension points were checked and the exact operation each cannot provide. That gives the provider a requirement it can act on without committing to your proposed internal implementation.

The project still needs a plan while the request is assessed. It may delay this feature, adjust the process, or use an edition-appropriate temporary exception with a retirement condition. Opening an API-gap ticket does not authorize direct table access, and it does not guarantee a delivery date. Keep the gap visible rather than hiding it inside a workaround.

Avoid this mistake
An API-gap ticket does not authorize direct table access or promise that the requested API will arrive by the project's deadline.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What evidence shows that existing APIs really do not fit?
  • How do you keep delivery moving without hiding the gap?
Strong answer criteria
  • Requests a supported business operation
  • Explains why supported alternatives do not fit
  • Defines what the project will do while waiting
Verification evidence
A clear API-gap record with searches for the target release, required operation and failure behavior, a reproducible example, and the chosen interim scope.

Read and verify
  • SAP extensibility options by environment and language version
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-08 | The business asks to reproduce a heavily customized legacy process exactly. How do you challenge that without dismissing the requirement?
column2:
Short answer
Separate the business result that must be preserved from the old screen or implementation. Demonstrate how standard configuration and supported extensions meet that result, including exception cases. Keep legal and contractual requirements explicit. Compare the ongoing cost of each retained customization with its value. Let the business owner decide using concrete behavior, cost, and risk rather than slogans.

Reasoning and example
The old approval screen combines several steps that standard applications separate. The real control may be that the requester cannot approve their own request and that every decision is recorded. Rebuilding the exact screen through internal hooks may add upgrade risk without improving either control. Walk through those requirements with the process owner.

Include unusual cases such as withdrawal, delegation, and rejected approvals so standard functionality is not accepted on a happy-path demo alone. Where a real requirement is missing, compare a supported extension or process adjustment with preserving the deviation. Fit-to-standard should help make that tradeoff visible, not dismiss a legitimate need or assume visual parity is the only measure of success.

Avoid this mistake
Fit-to-standard is not a slogan for refusing real requirements, and exact visual parity is not always the real business invariant.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which requirement is mandatory and who can prove it?
  • What exception case could invalidate the proposed standard process?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates outcomes from historical design
  • Uses concrete process demonstrations
  • Makes cost and ownership visible
Verification evidence
A fit-gap matrix with business-owner acceptance, exception-path demonstrations, and lifecycle cost estimates for retained deviations.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core dimensions beyond extensions
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-09 | Your team wants to release a custom API used by three other teams. What must be ready before setting its release state?
column2:
Short answer
Before release, define the API's supported inputs, outcomes, errors, transaction behavior, and permissions. Give it an owner willing to maintain compatibility. Keep stable types and behavior public and private storage details private. Capture a delivered baseline and set compatibility, deprecation, and successor rules. If the API is still experimental, coordinated component access may fit better than a premature stability promise.

Reasoning and example
Three teams already call a pricing API. Removing an optional field or changing rounding may look like cleanup to the provider but break one caller's business result. Keep a snapshot of what was delivered and use the applicable compatibility checks for detectable technical changes. Consumer tests cover meanings and outcomes that a signature comparison cannot prove.

Do not replace the old baseline just to silence a genuine incompatibility finding. Plan how current users migrate when a breaking change is needed, and communicate support periods. Supported access permission can enable internal collaboration, but releasing a stable API is a stronger ongoing commitment. Set the release state only when the provider is prepared to meet that commitment.

Avoid this mistake
Releasing an API is a provider commitment; broad access permission is not equivalent to a stable contract.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which changes can be detected statically and which need consumer tests?
  • How would you deprecate the API without breaking current users?
Strong answer criteria
  • Defines what the API owner must maintain
  • Keeps a trustworthy record of the delivered interface
  • Checks both technical compatibility and business behavior
Verification evidence
An API specification, owner and consumer list, prior-delivery snapshot, compatibility results, and consumer-contract test evidence.

Read and verify
  • SAP release contracts, visibility, and API lifecycle states
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.
  • SAP software component dependencies and compatibility snapshots
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-10 | The direct dependency scan is clean, but an upgrade still breaks the extension. What could the governance model be missing?
column2:
Short answer
Check what the scan did not cover: indirect calls, dynamic selection, configured implementations, remote interfaces, and data assumptions. Verify its package scope, check version, and classification data too. Connect static findings with a dependency map and process tests. Clean direct references are useful evidence, but they do not prove that every runtime path will survive an upgrade.

Reasoning and example
A custom facade chooses an internal implementation from configuration, so scanning only its direct references misses the actual dependency. A remote service can also change independently of the ABAP transport. Include these paths in the map and assign owners who can explain and test them.

Another upgrade failure may come from data behavior: a query expected one text row, but changed data now gives several and doubles a total. No forbidden direct call is needed for that defect. Rehearse representative configured processes on the target upgrade and document what the checks and tests covered. A green result is meaningful only within that stated scope; it is not proof that all hidden assumptions are safe.

Avoid this mistake
A green direct-reference check is not proof that the whole solution has no unsupported or semantically fragile dependencies.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you discover configuration-driven dependencies?
  • Which runtime paths must the upgrade rehearsal cover?
Strong answer criteria
  • Looks for indirect, dynamic, and configured dependencies
  • Checks whether the scan covered the needed objects
  • Tests complete business processes
Verification evidence
An expanded dependency graph, documented scan scope and tool versions, and upgrade regression evidence covering configured runtime paths.

Read and verify
  • SAP software component relations and consistency checks
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-11 | How would you enforce Clean Core in delivery without blocking every legacy transport immediately?
column2:
Short answer
Record existing findings as a clear baseline and prevent new unapproved risk. Use checks appropriate to the target environment for language, APIs, extension techniques, compatibility, security, and correctness. Keep existing exceptions bounded and prioritize their fixes. Make the gate's scope and thresholds reproducible. Give developers feedback early enough to fix issues before release day.

Reasoning and example
A layout change to a legacy report should not automatically demand an unplanned rewrite of the whole application. It also must not quietly introduce a new internal write dependency. Compare the current findings with the accepted baseline, then review new findings and any change that makes an existing exception riskier.

Store the check variant, versions, priorities, scope, and exception policy so teams cannot redefine green by weakening checks. Protect and review policy changes. Plan remediation for existing exposure with named owners instead of suppressing it forever. The baseline explains known risk; it is not permission to add unlimited new debt, and transport-blocking priorities are a configured team policy rather than universal ATC behavior.

Avoid this mistake
A baseline is not approval for unlimited new debt, and transport blocking thresholds are configured policy rather than a universal property of every ATC check.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What happens when a touched legacy dependency becomes riskier?
  • How do you stop teams from weakening the shared check variant?
Strong answer criteria
  • Distinguishes baseline from new risk
  • Uses reproducible early gates
  • Governs exception and policy changes
Verification evidence
A versioned gate policy, representative pass/fail cases, a protected check-configuration record, and a baseline-to-current findings comparison.

Read and verify
  • SAP ATC configuration and transport-release governance
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-12 | A vendor upgrade changes an object used by an approved Level C extension. How do you organize the response?
column2:
Short answer
Reassess the exception for the new vendor release. Find affected callers and processes, reproduce the failure, and compare old and new behavior. Check whether a suitable released replacement now exists. If the internal dependency remains justified, adapt its isolated boundary and test the full affected process. Coordinate vendor and custom delivery, including rollback or business recovery where data changes are involved.

Reasoning and example
An internal object's signature is unchanged, but its defaulting or validation now behaves differently. A syntax-only repair cannot show whether postings, permissions, messages, and resulting document states still meet the business need. In another case, activation fails because a type changed; fixing that type still needs behavioral regression tests.

Use the actual upgraded environment and record both vendor and custom source versions. Compare representative successful and rejected transactions, and investigate whether the defect depends on specific data. If a supported successor now covers the need, revisit keeping the exception at all. Last year's approval or successful upgrade is evidence about the previous situation, not a guarantee for this release.

Avoid this mistake
A previous exception or successful prior upgrade does not prove compatibility with the next vendor release.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How do you distinguish an API change from a data-dependent defect?
  • Would you keep the exception if a suitable released successor is now available?
Strong answer criteria
  • Reassesses release-specific exposure
  • Tests semantic behavior
  • Coordinates recovery and replacement
Verification evidence
A target-upgrade impact record, reproduced failure, reviewed boundary change, and process regression results tied to both vendor and custom revisions.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core levels, classic APIs, wrappers, and edition boundaries
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-13 | What would a credible two-year custom-code modernization roadmap look like?
column2:
Short answer
Build the roadmap around business capabilities and reduced maintenance risk. Retire confirmed unused functions, replace important risky dependencies, and use supported ABAP Cloud options for suitable new work. Valuable classic code can remain under clear governance. Give each phase owners, measurable outcomes, and operational acceptance. Reserve capacity for upgrades and API changes instead of promising a full RAP rewrite by a date.

Reasoning and example
One phase removes an unused interface after confirming business ownership. Another replaces internal reads with a released query. A third redesigns a critical posting path. These changes need different tests and deliver different benefits, so counting converted classes gives a poor picture of progress.

For each phase, say what risk or cost will decrease and how that will be demonstrated. Examples include fewer unsupported write paths, a successful target-upgrade rehearsal, or lower effort to adapt a shared interface. Budget for integration and operational acceptance, not only new screens. A roadmap can support gradual coexistence while still setting clear retirement goals for temporary bridges and unnecessary dependencies.

Avoid this mistake
Modernization is not measured reliably by RAP object count or by replacing all classic code regardless of business value.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What quarterly outcome would demonstrate reduced upgrade risk?
  • How do you fund remediation that has no visible new UI feature?
Strong answer criteria
  • Prioritizes outcomes for business capabilities
  • Keeps justified classic and modern code working together
  • Measures the reduction in maintenance and upgrade risk
Verification evidence
A capability-based roadmap with owners, usage decisions, target dependency reductions, migration acceptance criteria, and budgeted upgrade work.

Read and verify
  • SAP Clean Core dimensions beyond extensions
    Check three things separately: the dependency classification, its supported released use, and who approves and maintains any exception.

column1: GOV-14 | A classified classic API meets the need, while a released API covers only half the operation. Would you accept Level B?
column2:
Short answer
Yes, where the target permits it, a verified Level B API can be a reasonable choice. Compare the complete supported operation with the partial released alternative, including permissions, transaction safety, and maintenance. Verify the whole dependency path and state the B dependency honestly. Keep a reason to reassess later. This choice does not override Public Edition or restricted ABAP Cloud access rules.

Reasoning and example
The released API supports only part of the posting operation. Completing the rest with direct table updates may be less safe than using a properly classified classic API that performs the full transaction. Test the actual business result, required fields, rejection paths, and authorization rather than choosing a label without considering completeness.

Check the exact object's classification and extension technique; the name BAPI does not prove Level B. If the consumer uses a restricted language version, verify the allowed access design separately. Record why the decision fits this target and what successor or upgrade change would trigger review. Accepting B can be a responsible documented choice, but should never be presented as direct unrestricted Cloud access or an entirely A solution.

Avoid this mistake
Not every old API is Level B, and a Level B assessment does not make it directly callable from restricted ABAP Cloud code.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What makes the exact API qualify as classic rather than internal?
  • What would cause you to revisit this decision after an upgrade?
Strong answer criteria
  • Supports the Level B choice with exact evidence
  • Preserves the complete business transaction
  • Respects product and language restrictions
Verification evidence
Specific object-classification evidence, a complete operation test, a comparison with released alternatives, and a scheduled reassessment trigger.

column1: GOV-15 | A required report uses an internal read object with no current replacement. Would you accept Level C, and under what conditions?
column2:
Short answer
First prove that no suitable supported read meets the need and that the target allows the proposed use. If C is accepted, isolate the internal dependency, limit what callers depend on, and name its owner. Set a review trigger and replacement plan. Read-only reduces some write risks but still has confidentiality, result-correctness, and upgrade risks. Test those explicitly.

Reasoning and example
An internal view changes a join after an upgrade. The report still activates but now returns duplicate rows and a wrong business total. Another change could broaden returned data for a restricted user. A test that merely executes the SELECT successfully misses both problems.

Capture representative expected totals, row identities, filters, and denied-access results. Recheck them on the target release and use available SAP change information as supporting evidence, not a complete guarantee. Keep the exception tied to this precise dependency and purpose, with a date or event that forces review. A justified internal read is not blanket approval for other internal objects or non-recommended Level D techniques.

Avoid this mistake
Read-only does not mean risk-free, and Level C is not a blanket exemption for all internal objects or non-recommended Level D techniques.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What result change could escape an activation check?
  • Which precise event forces this exception back into review?
Strong answer criteria
  • Treats read semantics as consequential
  • Isolates and owns exposure
  • Defines focused compatibility evidence
Verification evidence
A bounded exception with dependency classification, authorization and result baselines, target-upgrade checks, and replacement-review triggers.

column1: GOV-16 | How would you assess a solution that uses a released CDS query, a classified classic BAPI, an internal class, and a modification?
column2:
Short answer
Assess each path separately on the actual target. The released query may support A use, the classified classic BAPI introduces B, the internal class introduces C, and a non-recommended modification can introduce D. Do not average them into one reassuring score. Link each to business use, ownership, and alternatives, then prioritize fixes using impact as well as classification.

Reasoning and example
The modification may sit in an old unused path, while the internal class is called during daily financial posting. Both dependencies belong in the factual assessment, but those usage differences affect what to fix first. Confirm historical and seasonal use with the process owner before deciding to remove anything.

For a replacement, test the full intended operation and its errors, not just successful activation. Keep the classification evidence, target version, owner, and business impact beside each finding. A single letter for the entire solution can hide these facts. Classification describes the exposure; remediation priority also needs use, criticality, available alternatives, and the cost of changing the business process safely.

Avoid this mistake
A single letter for a mixed solution can hide scope; classification and remediation priority are related but are not the same decision.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which capability would you remediate first and why?
  • What evidence is required before removing the modification?
Strong answer criteria
  • Classifies each dependency instead of averaging grades
  • Separates classification from fix priority
  • Uses business importance and actual usage
Verification evidence
A scoped assessment table linking each dependency to classification evidence, process impact, usage, ownership, and a justified remediation decision.

column1: GOV-17 | The sponsor says Clean Core is a developer concern and rejects funding for integration monitoring and data cleanup. How would you negotiate?
column2:
Short answer
Explain the business failures that monitoring and data quality prevent. Clean Core includes more than extension code: poor master data, unsupported integrations, and unmanaged process variants also make change difficult. Propose a small set of owned controls with clear outcomes and costs. Phase improvements where reasonable. Make any deferred business risk and its operating owner explicit.

Reasoning and example
An order API is properly released, but invalid customer mappings make messages fail repeatedly. Nobody owns the queue, so business orders remain incomplete even though the code uses supported interfaces. Another wrapper or ATC exception will not repair the mapping or ensure someone retries failed work.

Agree who maintains mappings, responds to alerts, reconciles results, and prioritizes cleanup. Use a concrete incident or realistic failure scenario to compare the cost of controls with the cost of unprocessed business work. Define measurable service expectations and distinguish essential controls from improvements that can wait. A good extensibility grade does not certify data quality, secure integration, or effective day-to-day operation.

Avoid this mistake
A strong extensibility classification does not certify clean data, standard processes, secure integrations, or effective operations.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • Which control delivers the highest near-term business value?
  • Who is accountable when an interface remains technically successful but business processing is incomplete?
Strong answer criteria
  • Connects monitoring and data controls to business results
  • Proposes a practical phased plan
  • Names business and operational owners
Verification evidence
A responsibility matrix, costed minimum control plan, measurable operational targets, and documented acceptance of deferred risks.

column1: GOV-18 | An interview panel shows an A-D chart with ATC priorities. What would you clarify before treating it as a release gate?
column2:
Short answer
Explain that the A-D priority mapping belongs to particular Clean Core checks. Ask which variant, checks, classification data, object scope, and target release produced the results. Other ATC priorities can describe security or performance issues instead. Define what the release gate proves, which exemptions remain, and which runtime tests are still needed. Save enough run information to repeat the assessment.

Reasoning and example
One project has fewer findings because its variant omitted an enhancement check or used different classification data. Comparing the raw count with another project can therefore reward missing checks rather than safer code. Store the configuration, source version, scope, and exemptions so the comparison is like for like.

Even matching static checks do not prove that a posting transaction behaves correctly. Add the relevant runtime evidence and distinguish a resolved dependency from a finding that was merely exempted. Do not treat every priority 1 as Level D or every priority 2 as C across all ATC checks. Absence of findings also does not prove complete Level A coverage when assessment scope is incomplete.

Avoid this mistake
Do not interpret every priority 1 finding as Level D, every priority 2 as Level C, or absence of findings as proof of complete Level A coverage.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • What would you store so this assessment can be reproduced?
  • How would you distinguish an exempted finding from a resolved dependency?
Strong answer criteria
  • Explains which check gives the priority mapping
  • Records enough information to repeat the assessment
  • Distinguishes static checks from runtime tests
Verification evidence
The exact ATC variant and check configuration, classification/version information, source and scope identifiers, exemptions, and complementary runtime validation results.
